short: A connection-oriented transport that delivers an ordered stream of bytes.
detail: TCP uses sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmissions to repair loss. The two directions have independent byte sequences.
design: A TCP ACK confirms receipt by the peer transport. Use an application acknowledgment when you need proof of processing or durability.

short: A connectionless transport that sends discrete datagrams.
detail: UDP provides ports, a length and a checksum, with no built-in retransmission, ordering, flow control or congestion control.
design: Choose UDP when late data has little value, or when an application protocol needs to control its own recovery. High-rate traffic still needs congestion control.

short: A TCP header and optional bytes sent as one network unit.
detail: A header carries flags, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, and the advertised receive window. A retransmission can contain the same byte range in a different segment.
design: Socket writes, wire segments and app reads can have different boundaries. Diagnose framing bugs at the byte-stream layer.

short: A separately addressed UDP message with a preserved boundary.
detail: One socket receive gets at most one datagram. If the application buffer is too small, the datagram can be truncated.
design: Size messages to fit the path MTU when possible. IP fragmentation makes a datagram depend on delivery of every fragment.

short: TCP preserves byte order while the application defines where each message starts and ends.
detail: Two writes can arrive in one read, and one write can span multiple reads. Framing adds a convention such as a length prefix, delimiter or fixed size.
design: Make parsers incremental and cap frame sizes. Test split headers and multiple frames in a single read.

short: SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK establish a TCP connection.
detail: Both peers learn each other’s ISN and can negotiate options such as MSS and SACK support. The server reaches ESTABLISHED on receipt of the third segment.
design: Budget a round trip before a client can send ordinary data. Warm connections help latency-sensitive paths, especially across regions.

short: The TCP flag that synchronizes the sender’s initial sequence number.
detail: A normal active open starts with a SYN carrying the client ISN. SYN consumes one sequence number before the first payload byte.
design: A missing response to a SYN is a different failure mode from an explicit refusal. Diagnose the initial exchange before tuning application retries.

short: The server’s SYN and its acknowledgment of the client’s SYN, carried together.
detail: The peer advertises its own ISN and returns the client ISN plus one as the ACK number.
design: If a trace shows repeated SYNs and outgoing SYN-ACKs, inspect the return path and the final ACK before blaming application startup.

short: An ACK number specifies the next sequence number the receiver expects.
detail: It cumulatively covers all bytes before that number in this direction. SACK can describe blocks beyond the first gap. Pure ACKs consume no sequence space.
design: A stalled ACK with rising SACK coverage points to a missing range. A falling advertised window points to a receiver that cannot drain fast enough.

short: FIN says that the sender has finished its direction of the stream.
detail: FIN follows previously queued bytes and consumes one sequence number. The other direction can remain open until the peer sends its own FIN.
design: If a protocol treats end of stream as a request boundary, half-close lets the client finish its write while still reading the response.

short: The TCP reset flag rejects or aborts a connection.
detail: A SYN sent to a closed port commonly receives RST-ACK. An in-window reset on an existing connection can abort it without the orderly FIN exchange.
design: Distinguish immediate refusal or reset from a timeout. The symptoms point to different failure locations and have different retry costs.

short: The starting sequence number a TCP endpoint announces in its SYN.
detail: Each direction has its own ISN. The first data byte starts at ISN plus one.
design: Packet analyzers often normalize sequence numbers. Know whether a trace uses raw or relative numbers before comparing captures.

short: The position of a byte range in one direction of a TCP stream.
detail: Data advances the number by the payload length, SYN and FIN advance it by one, and a retry reuses the sequence range.
design: Sequence ranges tell you whether the sender released new bytes, retried a gap, or waited on flow control.

short: A local port usually allocated automatically for an outbound connection.
detail: TCP identity includes both IP addresses and both ports. For one source IP and one destination tuple, the usable local range can cap simultaneous and recently closed connections.
design: At high connection churn, check client or NAT port availability and connection lifetimes before raising server concurrency.

short: The active closer retains TCP state after sending the final ACK.
detail: The nominal interval is 2MSL. The retained state can acknowledge a repeated FIN and allows old segments to expire before reuse of the same connection identity.
design: Estimate the port demand from close rate times retention time. Connection reuse reduces churn without weakening close safety.

short: The maximum time TCP assumes an old segment can remain in the network.
detail: An orderly active close waits two MSLs. The lab uses a compressed MSL of one second to make the release visible. Operating systems use their own retention timings.
design: Measure the actual platform’s TIME_WAIT retention before sizing the outbound connection budget.

short: Send more than one request over an already established connection.
detail: A pool keeps a bounded set of live connections to reuse. The lab uses a one-connection pool and runs its requests serially.
design: Set pool size and queue limits together. Reuse saves handshake work and ports, while too small a pool can add request wait time.

short: The maximum payload size of an ordinary TCP segment for a sender.
detail: Peers advertise receive MSS in SYNs. The effective send MSS also depends on path and header overhead. The lab uses 1460 bytes.
design: Tunnels and extra headers can reduce payload per packet. When sizing a window, convert segments to bytes using the effective MSS.

short: The elapsed time for traffic to reach the peer and its response to return.
detail: Propagation, queueing and receiver behavior can all affect observed samples. The congestion chart separates base RTT from illustrative queueing.
design: RTT establishes the price of each handshake or feedback round. It also determines how many bytes a window-limited flow needs in flight.

short: The sender’s deadline for retrying the oldest unacknowledged bytes without other loss evidence.
detail: Real TCP estimates it from smoothed RTT and variability, and doubles it on successive expirations. The lab uses a shorter illustrative starting RTO.
design: Sparse requests and tail losses can miss the duplicate ACK threshold, so retransmission timers can dominate tail latency.

short: An ACK that repeats the same cumulative number without advancing the window.
detail: An out-of-order segment can elicit a duplicate ACK. Reordering can also generate duplicates, so one repeat is weak loss evidence.
design: Correlate repeated ACKs with sequence gaps, SACK blocks and RTT before treating them as proof of congestion.

short: Classic TCP retries a missing segment after three duplicate ACKs.
detail: The duplicate ACKs imply that later data reached the receiver. Modern implementations can also use time-based loss detection and selective recovery.
design: Short or tail-loss-heavy transfers may have too little data after the gap to trigger this path. Watch timeout and fast-retry counters separately.

short: A TCP option reporting received byte ranges beyond the cumulative ACK.
detail: Each SACK block gives the first byte and the exclusive right edge of a contiguous range. SACK reports receipt without advancing the cumulative ACK through a gap.
design: On a large flight with multiple losses, selective recovery can repair missing ranges without resending everything beyond the first gap.

short: The receiver keeps unread and out-of-order bytes in bounded socket storage.
detail: An unread contiguous range consumes receive-window space. Out-of-order segments occupy positions in the already advertised sequence range until the gap fills.
design: Inspect app read cadence and socket buffer pressure together. More receive memory can absorb a burst, but it cannot fix sustained consumer lag.

short: How many bytes the peer offers to accept starting at the cumulative ACK.
detail: The sender must stay inside the advertised right edge as well as its own congestion window. The window can reopen after application reads.
design: A large congestion window cannot overcome a receiver with no room. Separate network bottlenecks from flow-control stalls.

short: The receiver advertises no room for new stream bytes.
detail: The sender stops ordinary new data. A window update or probe response advertises fresh space after the receiver drains.
design: A live socket can show no progress because its app stopped reading. Alert on useful app progress as well as connection health.

short: A small transmission that asks the peer to report its receive window again.
detail: TCP can send or retransmit an octet despite a zero window. The peer ACKs with its current window, and probe spacing backs off while it stays closed.
design: The probe recovers from a lost window update. It cannot make a stalled application read, so client deadlines still matter.

short: TCP can buffer a small write while earlier data is unacknowledged.
detail: It can send again when data is acknowledged or when it accumulates enough bytes for a full segment. A delayed ACK can add a visible wait for a small second write.
design: Batch logically related writes at the application boundary, or consider TCP_NODELAY for a measured small-message latency problem.

short: A receiver briefly holds an ACK so one ACK can cover more data.
detail: The lab ACKs the second in-order segment immediately or waits up to 40 ms for a lone segment. Real timer and ACK policies vary by stack and traffic.
design: Small back-to-back writes can wait on the interaction with Nagle. Measure the actual timer pattern before attributing every latency bump to it.

short: A socket option that disables Nagle’s wait on small TCP writes.
detail: It lets queued small payloads send immediately when the send and receive windows allow. Delayed ACK remains a receiver policy.
design: Use it for latency-sensitive small writes when justified. More packets per byte can increase host CPU and link overhead.

short: The sender’s estimate of how much unacknowledged data the path can handle.
detail: A sender is constrained by cwnd and rwnd. With ample receive window and offered data, cwnd divided by RTT approximates the window-limited send rate.
design: Capacity, RTT, receiver limits and the sender’s current window can all cap throughput. Inspect each before you buy bandwidth.

short: An ACK-driven phase that grows the congestion window rapidly from a small initial value.
detail: With one ACK per full segment the window can roughly double per RTT until a threshold or congestion event. Actual initial windows and startup algorithms vary.
design: Short transfers can end before they fully use the path. Connection reuse and smaller responses can matter more than peak link capacity.

short: The window level at which classic growth changes from slow start to congestion avoidance.
detail: Loss recovery can lower it based on the earlier outstanding flight. The lab starts at 16 MSS for readability.
design: Separate a startup stall from steady-state loss when analyzing small transfers. Their recovery time and tuning levers differ.

short: The phase that searches for more capacity more cautiously than slow start.
detail: Reno adds about one MSS per RTT during a healthy round. Other controllers use different growth and loss rules.
design: A linear ramp takes more wall time on high-RTT paths. Judge transfer recovery in milliseconds as well as rounds.

short: Reno’s congestion window grows additively and shrinks multiplicatively after a congestion signal.
detail: A saturated flight grows roughly one MSS per RTT, and a loss handled by fast recovery roughly halves it. An RTO invokes a more severe reset.
design: The sawtooth trades throughput for stability and sharing. Longer RTT means each additive step takes longer.

short: A loss-based controller with a cubic window target over elapsed time.
detail: It normally keeps about 70% of the prior window after a congestion event. The cubic target approaches the prior peak gently and grows faster past it. Real implementations include safeguards absent from this lab.
design: CUBIC helps probing on high-bandwidth, long-distance paths. Compare recovery, latency and fairness under the expected traffic mix.

short: A congestion controller that models bottleneck bandwidth and propagation RTT.
detail: BBR estimates delivery rate and minimum RTT, then varies pacing and flight to test the path. Version-specific behavior also considers loss and inflight bounds.
design: Evaluate an algorithm against the queues, competing flows and tail-latency goals of your path. A higher average goodput alone can miss user-visible regressions.

short: The amount of data in flight needed to fill a path at its bottleneck rate over one base RTT.
detail: Multiply bottleneck bits per second by base RTT in seconds, then divide by eight for bytes. More flight than the BDP can occupy queues.
design: Long paths need bigger windows at the same bandwidth. Size buffers and parallelism against actual RTT and capacity.

short: Excessive queue delay from persistently filled network buffers.
detail: Flight above the unqueued BDP can back up at the bottleneck. A large queue may keep throughput high while making RTT much worse.
design: Measure loaded RTT alongside throughput. Queue management and pacing can improve interactive latency on a shared link.

short: A secure transport over UDP with its own reliability and congestion control.
detail: QUIC is often implemented in user space. It acknowledges QUIC packets and retransmits lost stream data as needed, with ordering scoped to each stream.
design: QUIC offers independent streams on one connection, while the UDP substrate still needs path validation, pacing and mature loss recovery.
